label: thm:main
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:main}
For every integer $n\geq2$, the identity
\begin{equation}\label{eq:identity}
\mathbf p\approx\mathbf p+bxe
\end{equation}
holds in $\mathbf M_n(S_7)$ if and only if $n=2$.
Consequently,
\[
\mathsf V(\mathbf M_2(S_7))<\mathsf V(\mathbf M_n(S_7))
\qquad\text{for every }n\geq3.
\]
head: environment

label: lem:cube
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $1\leq i,j\leq n$, we have
\[
(A^3)_{ij}=\sum_{k,l=1}^n A_{ik}A_{kl}A_{lj}.
\]
If $(A^3)_{ij}=1$, every summand is $1$ by~\eqref{eq:flat}.
In particular, $A_{kl}=1$ for all $k,l$, and hence $A=J_n$.

Suppose that $(A^3)_{ij}=a$. Taking $k=l=i$ gives
$A_{ii}^2A_{ij}=a$. Thus $A_{ii}=1$ and $A_{ij}=a$.
However, the summand with $k=j$ and $l=i$ is
$A_{ij}A_{ji}A_{ij}=\infty$, a contradiction.
Therefore $A^3$ has no entry equal to $a$. If $A\neJ_n$, it also
has no entry equal to $1$, so $A^3=\Omega_n$.
The equality $J_n^3=J_n$ is immediate.
head: environment

label: lem:factor
title: Lemma
head: environment

label: eq:pair
title: Proof
body_md:
If $XY=J_n$, then~\eqref{eq:flat} gives $X_{rk}Y_{ks}=1$
for all $r,k,s$. Both factors must be $1$, proving the first assertion.

Suppose that $XY=K_n$. Again by~\eqref{eq:flat},
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pair}
X_{rk}Y_{ks}=a\qquad(1\leq r,k,s\leq n).
\end{equation}
Fix $k$ and set $u_k=X_{1k}$. Equation~\eqref{eq:pair} implies
that $u_k\in\{1,a\}$ and $Y_{ks}=\overline{u_k}$ for every $s$.
Using $s=1$ in~\eqref{eq:pair} then yields $X_{rk}=u_k$ for
every $r$. This proves~\eqref{eq:profile}.
Conversely,~\eqref{eq:profile} makes every summand in each entry
of $XY$ equal to $a$, and hence $XY=K_n$.

label: lem:embedding
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $E,B,X,Y,Z$ be arbitrary matrices in $\mathbf M_2(S_7)$, and put
\[
F=E^3BE^3+EXYE+BX+YE+Z^2.
\]
We prove $F=F+BXE$ entrywise. Fix $i,j\in\{1,2\}$.
If $F_{ij}=\infty$, then $(F+BXE)_{ij}=F_{ij}$ automatically.
Suppose, therefore, that
\[
F_{ij}=c\in\{1,a\}.
\]
By~\eqref{eq:flat}, each of the five summands defining $F$ has
$(i,j)$-entry equal to $c$.

Since $(E^3BE^3)_{ij}=c$, Lemma~\ref{lem:cube} implies $E=J_2$:
otherwise $E^3BE^3=\Omega_2$. Applying~\eqref{eq:sandwich} to
the first two summands gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:reduction}
B=[c]_2,\qquad XY=[c]_2.
\end{equation}
We consider the two possible values of $c$.

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{Case 1: $c=1$.}
By~\eqref{eq:reduction} and Lemma~\ref{lem:factor}(1),
$B=X=Y=J_2$. Hence $BXE=J_2$, so $(BXE)_{ij}=F_{ij}$.

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{Case 2: $c=a$.}
Now $B=K_2$ and $XY=K_2$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:factor}(2),
there exist $u_1,u_2\in\{1,a\}$ such that
\[
X_{rk}=u_k,\qquad Y_{ks}=\overline{u_k}
\qquad(r,k,s\in\{1,2\}).
\]
The third and fourth summands in $F$ yield
\[
a=(BX)_{ij}=a u_j,
\qquad
a=(YE)_{ij}=\overline{u_i}.
\]
Consequently,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:endpoints}
u_i=u_j=1.
\end{equation}

The fifth summand gives $(Z^2)_{ij}=a$. This forces $i\ne j$.
Indeed, if $i=j$, the expansion of $(Z^2)_{ii}$ contains the summand
$Z_{ii}^2\in\{1,\infty\}$, contrary to~\eqref{eq:flat}.
Since the index set has only two elements, $\{i,j\}=\{1,2\}$.
It follows from~\eqref{eq:endpoints} that $u_1=u_2=1$, and hence
$X=J_2$. Thus $BXE=K_2$, giving $(BXE)_{ij}=F_{ij}$ in this
case as well.

In every case, $(F+BXE)_{ij}=F_{ij}$. Since $i,j$ were arbitrary,
$F=F+BXE$, as required.
head: environment

label: prop:higher
title: Proposition
head: environment

label: eq:general-witness
title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $n\geq3$. Set $u_3=a$ and $u_k=1$ for $k\ne3$, and take
$E=J_n$, $B=K_n$. Define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-witness}
X_{rk}=u_k,\qquad Y_{ks}=\overline{u_k},\qquad
Z_{rs}=\begin{cases}
a,&s=2\text{ and }r\ne2,\\
1,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\end{equation}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:factor}, $XY=K_n$, and hence
\[
E^3BE^3=EXYE=K_n.
\]
Since $u_1=u_2=1$, we also have
\[
(BX)_{12}=\sum_{k=1}^n a u_2=a,
\qquad
(YE)_{12}=\sum_{k=1}^n\overline{u_1}=a.
\]
For the square term, every summand at coordinate $(1,2)$ equals $a$:
\[
Z_{1k}Z_{k2}=
\begin{cases}
a\cdot1,&k=2,\\
1\cdot a,&k\ne2.
\end{cases}
\]
Thus $(Z^2)_{12}=a$. If $F$ is the value of $\mathbf p$ under this
substitution, all five summands have $(1,2)$-entry $a$, so $F_{12}=a$.

On the other hand, $u_3=a$ gives $(BX)_{i3}=a u_3=\infty$
for every $i$. Each entry of $BXE$ therefore contains the summand
$(BX)_{i3}E_{3j}=\infty$, and hence $BXE=\Omega_n$.
Consequently, $(F+BXE)_{12}=\infty\ne a=F_{12}$, proving the claim.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Propositions~\ref{prop:two} and~\ref{prop:higher} establish the
assertion about~\eqref{eq:identity}. By Lemma~\ref{lem:embedding},
$\mathbf M_2(S_7)$ embeds into $\mathbf M_n(S_7)$ for every $n\geq3$,
so $\mathsf V(\mathbf M_2(S_7))\leq\mathsf V(\mathbf M_n(S_7))$.
Every member of $\mathsf V(\mathbf M_2(S_7))$ satisfies~\eqref{eq:identity},
whereas $\mathbf M_n(S_7)$ does not. The inclusion is therefore strict.
